When Brazil's [first round
results](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/flavio-bolsonaro-after-the-first-
round-against-lula-brazil-wants-
change/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX09XTFRBQzdGVzFLVFBaS0lWU0o3QTQxWFFCNTZVNVQ)
came out, the Brazilian left went into a panic. Pollsters undercounted far-
right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro's tally, who ended up first with 47% of the
vote. Brazil's president, Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva, a veritable legend of the
Latin American left, fell to second place, with 45%, a difference of over 2
million votes. Sentiment around Brazil's left electorate was negative and
defeatist. It seemed quite impossible to turn around such a solid Bolsonaro
advantage.

But just when morale was at its lowest, Lula reshuffled his campaign team,
incorporating the 41-year-old Governor of Piaui State, Rafael Fonteles. Lula,
now in his 80s, had never been much for social media, seeing it as a
U.S.-backed fake news industry that could never replace face-to-face contact
with his voters. Fonteles' [greatest
achievement](https://valorinternational.globo.com/politics/news/2026/10/19/new-
advisers-give-lulas-reelection-campaign-fresh-momentum.ghtml) was convincing
Lula he could do both: an aggressive social media campaign, while travelling
the country.

Thus, Lula's revamped campaign launched two days later, with the
octogenarian's first-ever [selfie
video](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeMf9IPt4_j/?mdxt=bHMxMjByOW5sbnln).
This new approach was new ground for Lula. According to insiders, Lula has
historically preferred a more sober tone and highly produced aesthetic focused
on reporting his achievements to the public. The strategy was simply no longer
working with newer generations that sought a personal connection and a vision
for the future. Fonteles' new aesthetic was bare-bones - the man himself,
holding his own phone, with no tie, just talking to people not about legacy,
but things that matter today: ending Brazil's [44-hour work-
week](https://apnews.com/article/brazil-workweek-lula-flavio-bolsonaro-
senate-b851c95d90ff5ad3675e4ec343bd12fe), free buses on weekends, and
protecting social programmes from Bolsonaro's Milei-inspired austerity plans.
It was a style that worked for Lula and a message that resonated with Brazil.
You could say Fonteles learned the right lessons from Zohran Mamdani's
success: not that flashy fonts and engaging videos win elections; but that his
job was to make the voter pay attention to the message, whatever that meant.
And oh did he!
